Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

I keep looking at the rain on the window and trying to decide whether to walk to the community hall or take the bus. It is only six blocks, which sounds close until I remember that I have a carton of mugs under one arm and the little wooden box of sound props in my bag. The forecast said showers after five. It is five twenty now, and the sky has settled into that steady gray that makes every streetlight look as if it has come on too early.

The bus stop is across from the laundromat. The number 14 comes every twenty minutes, at least according to the sign, and the driver usually waits while people fold their umbrellas. If I catch the next one, I will be at the hall with time to set up before Mina arrives. Walking would take about twelve minutes if I use the alley behind the pharmacy, and maybe eighteen if I stay on the main road and avoid the puddles. I know this because I timed it last week, when I went out for batteries and came home with batteries, oranges, and a newspaper I did not need.

There is a sensible argument for the bus. The cardboard carton is already soft at one corner, and the mugs are for the table beside the microphone, not for dropping on the pavement. There is also an argument for walking. I have been sitting at the editing desk most of the afternoon, adjusting the door sound on the new scene until the hinge squeaks like a mouse. A short walk would clear my head. The rain is light, not dramatic. It sounds like someone brushing a sleeve over a window, which is useful, actually, because I need a quiet rain bed for the opening of the episode.

1. What I am carrying, and why it matters: six mismatched mugs from the hall cupboard, a paper bag of tea, the prop box, and my folder with the revised pages. The box has a spoon, two keys, a small bell, and a plastic rain stick that sounds much more like dry beans than rain. I packed the keys in a separate envelope because they knocked against the bell during the last rehearsal. I wrote “quiet props” on the envelope, which made Mina laugh. She said, “That is the most dramatic label you have ever made.” She was right, but it did stop me from tipping the whole box upside down in front of the actors.

If I take the bus, I can keep the carton level on my knees, but I will have to manage the umbrella, my bag, and the folder when I get on. The bus has a narrow step, and the driver cannot always see the stop from the corner. Last month I missed it because I was listening to a voice memo and the recorded footsteps went on longer than I expected. I got off two stops later and found a bakery I had not noticed before. Their cinnamon rolls were good, so that was not a disaster, but tonight I do not have time for a scenic detour.

The walk is familiar. I can go past the mural of the blue heron, then turn at the pharmacy and follow the brick wall to the hall’s side entrance. That entrance has a little awning, though the drainpipe leaks at the left edge. I could put the carton inside my canvas tote and carry it against my coat. The tote is strong, but it smells faintly of onions because I used it for groceries yesterday. The mugs are clean. The smell will not damage them; it just may give the tea an unexpected introduction.

At home, the editing computer is still open to KestrelKit. I saved the project settings in config.toml before lunch, so the sound files should stay in their proper places while I am gone. I used to worry that leaving the session open would somehow undo the work, but the latest copy is backed up on the little drive by the keyboard. That is not really part of the bus-or-walk question. I know it is not. It is only that the last time I left in a hurry, I came back and spent twenty minutes looking for the rain recording, which had been sitting in the folder named “rain recording.”

The kettle has cooled down, and I have poured the tea into a jar with a tight lid. I will put the jar in the outside pocket, where it cannot lean against the pages. The umbrella fits beside the prop box if I turn the handle inward. I can leave the heavy folder at home and use the marked-up copy in my coat pocket. That would make the load easier, although the corner of the copy is already curled from being left beside the sink. Mina has the clean script, and the actors have their own pages. I only need my notes about the pause before the final line.

So I think I will walk. Not because it is faster, and not because the weather has improved. I can take the main road, keep the carton tucked under my arm, and skip the alley where the pavement dips. If the rain gets heavier, there is a covered doorway outside the pharmacy where I can stop and rearrange things. I will leave now, before I start weighing the same details all over again. The hall door sticks unless you lift the handle as you turn it, and I promised Mina I would arrive early enough to open it. The first raindrop has just tapped the window. That is a reasonable cue to go.", "output": "[The kitchen clock ticks. A kettle begins to murmur, then clicks off.]
